memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: Do not plant two kinds of seed in your vineyard; if you do, not only the crops you plant but also the fruit of the vineyard will be defiled. Do not plow with an ox and a donkey yoked together. Do not wear clothes of wool and linen woven together. - Deut 22:9-11 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
These laws about not mixing seeds, not yoking an ox with a donkey, and not weaving wool with linen can seem strange to us. Their deeper purpose was to teach Israel, in vivid everyday ways, that they were a people set apart, called to a life that was distinct and undivided. Each small act of daily life became a reminder that they belonged wholly to God and were not to blend His ways with the ways of the surrounding nations.

We are not bound by these particular ceremonial laws today. The New Testament makes clear that such regulations were shadows pointing forward, and believers are not required to keep them (Col 2:16-17). But the principle behind them still speaks. God calls His people to a life that is wholehearted and set apart, not mixing devotion to Him with the values of a world that does not honour Him.

Think about the image of an ox and donkey yoked together, pulling unevenly, struggling against each other. That pictures the difficulty of a divided life, trying to serve God while also being pulled by opposing values. Paul later used similar imagery to warn against being "unequally yoked" with what pulls us from Christ (2 Cor 6:14). God invites us into a whole, undivided devotion to Him. Where do you sense a "mixing" in your life that God is calling you to make whole?

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Where do you feel pulled in two directions spiritually?
2. What does wholehearted devotion to God look like for you?
3. How can you live "set apart" without becoming self-righteous?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Lord, free me from a divided heart. Help me live wholeheartedly for You, set apart and undivided in my devotion. Amen.
